note: As a reply, usually lukewarm: 还好吧 means "it's okay", short of praise. A polite way to avoid saying something is good or bad.
An everyday word, not a clinical one: 嗓子发炎 is a sore throat and 伤口发炎 is an infected cut.
Usually disapproving: 安插亲信 means slotting one's own people into posts through connections.
Used for spies and informers placed in secret: 安插眼线 ("plant an informer"), 安插卧底 ("plant a mole").
A standard report workers and students are expected to write: 年终总结 is the year-end review of one's own work, often required by employers.
At work, passing probation to become a regular employee. In the Communist Party, a probationary member becoming a full member.
Usually with 了: 他已经不在了 ("he's no longer with us"). A gentle way to mention a death, common in speech.

gloss: the five social insurances (pension, medical, unemployment, work injury and maternity)
note: Employers are legally required to pay these, usually mentioned as 五险一金 with the housing fund added. Job ads list it as a basic benefit.
Can sound like a challenge: 你是什么人？ demands to know someone's standing. 他是你什么人？ asks how someone is related to the listener.

gloss: to handle; to transact; to conduct
note: The standard verb for paperwork at banks and government offices: 办理手续 ("go through the formalities"), 办理业务.
请你吃饭 means the speaker is paying. Older people still greet with 吃饭了吗？ as a hello rather than a question.
Usually in 靠……吃饭: 靠手艺吃饭 ("live by one's craft"), 靠脸吃饭 ("get by on looks").
Usually 心里嘀咕 or 犯嘀咕: having doubts or misgivings that one keeps to oneself.
At New Year, 回家 usually means travelling back to one's hometown and parents: 回家过年.
The highest level of schooling completed (本科, 硕士), which employers screen on closely. Separate from 学位, the degree actually awarded.
Mostly about manners. 没教养 is a strong insult that reflects on how someone's parents raised them.
The official name in mainland China for standard Mandarin. Taiwan calls it 国语 and Singapore 华语.

gloss: lit. fish sink, goose alights (idiom, from Zhuangzi 莊子|庄子[Zhuang1 zi3]); fig. female beauty captivating even the birds and beasts
note: A classical compliment for a woman's beauty, often paired with 闭月羞花. Later stories link it to the ancient beauties Xi Shi and Wang Zhaojun.

gloss: fixed government purchase (esp of farm products)
note: A planned-economy term: the state set quotas of grain, pigs and other farm goods that producers had to sell to it at fixed prices.
Also the usual word for strays: 流浪猫 and 流浪狗 are stray cats and dogs. 流浪汉 is a homeless man.
In entertainment news, a young actress or singer with a pure, innocent image: 玉女明星.
Suggests greedy carving up by stronger parties, as when foreign powers sought to 瓜分中国 in the late Qing. Apps also use it for prize pools: 瓜分百万红包.
看人脸色 means having to watch someone's moods to stay in their favour; 给人脸色看 means showing displeasure through one's expression.

gloss: to compensate for working on a holiday by resting on a workday
note: Part of the official holiday system, where weekends are turned into workdays to make longer breaks. The practice draws frequent complaints.
Often means taking someone's place under false pretences: 冒名顶替. Cases of people taking others' university places this way have caused public outrage.
Ordinary people as opposed to officials. 老百姓 is how people describe themselves in contrast to those in power, and officials use it too.
Also means time: 没功夫 ("no time"), 一会儿功夫 ("a moment"). 下功夫 means putting real effort into something.
Also a polite title for people in the arts, media and other fields who don't teach: 王老师 can be a TV host or an editor.
方便吗？ asks whether now is a good time, for a call or a visit. 不方便 is a polite way to decline without giving a reason.
Mostly comes before something unwelcome: 有点贵 ("a bit pricey"), 有点累 ("a bit tired").
Often means "probably": 应该没问题 ("it should be fine"). 应该的 is a modest reply to thanks: "it was the least I could do".
Also praises things done well: 干得漂亮 ("nicely done"). 说漂亮话 means saying nice-sounding things without meaning them.
After an adjective it means "extremely": 累得不行 ("exhausted"). 他快不行了 can mean he is dying.
An approving word in official histories: 农民起义 ("peasant uprising"). Rebellions seen as illegitimate are called 叛乱 instead.
After the gaokao, 填志愿 means listing one's preferred universities and majors in ranked order; 第一志愿 is the first choice.
公主病 describes a spoiled young woman who expects to be pampered. In KTV venues 公主 is also a euphemism for a hostess.
Often a required registration with the authorities: websites in mainland China must display an ICP 备案 number.
Covers official review of books, films, games and online posts, before or after release. 过审 means passing it.
讨个说法 means pressing those responsible, often officials or a company, to explain and make things right.

gloss: successful candidate in the highest imperial civil service examination
note: The top degree of the imperial examinations, decided by the palace exam in the capital, and the usual route to high office.
Children also call any elderly man 爷爷, and 老爷爷 is a polite way to refer to an old man in general.
Children also call any elderly woman 奶奶, and 老奶奶 is a polite way to refer to an old woman in general.
In Mao-era politics a label of attack, as in 资产阶级思想 ("bourgeois thinking"). 小资, short for 小资产阶级, now means someone with refined middle-class tastes.
In speech it often just means "probably": 估计他不来了, "he's probably not coming".
Long the standard mainland word for husband or wife. Younger speakers more often say 老公 or 老婆, and forms use 配偶.
Someone who acts like a lord expecting to be served. 别把自己当大爷 means "stop acting like you own the place".

gloss: term of respect for older man
note: The usual way to address an old man in the north, stranger or not: 大爷，去车站怎么走？ "Excuse me, sir, how do I get to the station?"

gloss: aunt (affectionate term for an elderly woman)
note: The usual way to address a middle-aged or older woman in the north. In the media, 中国大妈 is a collective label for such women, as shoppers or square dancers.

gloss: to feel jealous (esp. because of a rival in love or affection)
note: Literally "eat vinegar". Often light and teasing, said of partners or of a child jealous of a new sibling.

gloss: to convalesce for a month following childbirth, following a special diet, and observing various taboos to protect the body from exposure to the "wind"
note: Still widely observed: new mothers are often told not to wash their hair, bathe or go outdoors. Paid 月子中心 (postpartum centres) are common in cities.
喝喜酒 means attending a wedding. 什么时候请我们喝喜酒？ is a teasing way of asking someone when they will get married.

gloss: gift money (on the occasion of a wedding etc)
note: Cash given at weddings and similar events, with the amount set by closeness and local custom. Rising amounts are a common complaint.

gloss: money given to children as a gift on Chinese New Year's Eve
note: Given by elders in red envelopes. Parents often take it to keep "for later", a long-running family joke.
Given as gifts to family, colleagues and clients before the festival. Lavish gift boxes have drawn official criticism for extravagance.

gloss: glutinous rice and choice of filling wrapped in leaves and steamed or boiled
note: The food of the Dragon Boat Festival. Whether the filling should be sweet or savoury is a running north-south argument online.
Often based on one's birth date and hour (八字). Some families still consult a fortune-teller about marriage matches or wedding dates.

gloss: year of one's birth sign, according to the cycle of 12 animals of the earthly branches 地支[di4 zhi1]
note: Traditionally an unlucky year, so people wear red underwear, belts or bracelets to ward off bad luck.
Covers scalpers of train tickets, concert tickets and hospital appointment slips. A gang of them is 黄牛党.
Used for cheap clones of brand phones and then for any knockoff or parody. Can be playful as well as dismissive: 山寨版 ("knockoff version").
In revolutionary language, a rural landlord or strongman; the slogan 打土豪，分田地 called for seizing their land.
Someone with lots of money and showy taste. Often joking: 土豪，我们做朋友吧 ("rich guy, let's be friends").

gloss: "Mr Perfect" (i.e. tall, rich and handsome) (Internet slang)
note: An online label for the ideal suitor, often used mockingly, and set against the self-mocking 屌丝 ("loser").

gloss: "Ms Perfect" (i.e. fair-skinned, rich and beautiful) (Internet slang)
note: The female counterpart of 高富帅. 白 is there because pale skin is widely prized as a beauty standard.

gloss: (on social media) to check in to a location
note: Also visiting a trendy place to take photos and post them: 网红打卡地 ("a spot famous online"). Daily habit check-ins are called 打卡 too.
网红店 and 网红餐厅 are places made popular online, often with long queues. The label can suggest style over substance.

gloss: (neologism) (slang) to spark interest in a product or idea (esp. on social media)
note: Shopping slang from social media: 被种草 means being made to want something, and 拔草 means buying it or losing interest.

gloss: (neologism c. 2016) (slang) to watch an entertaining spectacle from the sidelines and-or engage in gossip about it
note: From 吃瓜群众 ("melon-eating masses"), bystanders following celebrity scandals online. Said of oneself, it signals curiosity without taking sides.
An online insult for someone who argues with everything for its own sake, from 抬杠 ("to bicker").
Northeastern slang spread by livestreaming apps, where hosts call viewers 老铁. 老铁，没毛病 means "bro, no problem".
Literally "little fresh meat": a young, good-looking male star. Can be admiring or a jab at young actors seen as all looks and no skill.

gloss: children of entrepreneurs who became wealthy under Deng Xiaoping's economic reforms in the 1980s
note: Now used of any rich family's children, usually with an image of entitlement and showy spending.
Common in stories about privilege. The 我爸是李刚 ("my dad is Li Gang") case made it a byword for using a parent's power to escape consequences.

gloss: (slang) to rely on one's father's wealth or prestige to get ahead
note: Said resentfully of competition decided by family background, not effort: 这年头还得拼爹 ("these days it comes down to who your dad is").

gloss: (coll.) to live with and depend on one's parents even upon reaching adulthood
note: Literally "gnaw on the old", and disapproving. 啃老族 is the label for adults who live off their parents.

gloss: no-frills civil wedding ceremony lacking a material foundation: no car, house, reception, rings, or honeymoon
note: Marrying without the flat, car and big wedding that families often expect. Can be a stand against those expectations or simply what a couple can afford.
A common self-description among urban homeowners paying decades-long mortgages. Owning a flat is widely seen as a precondition for marriage.

gloss: a residential property located within the designated catchment area of a desirable school, often sought after by parents to secure school admission for their children
note: These flats can cost far more than homes nearby, since public school places depend on where a family owns its home.
Mostly ordered through apps such as Meituan; 点外卖 ("order delivery") is an everyday habit, and couriers are called 外卖小哥.

gloss: Moments (social networking function of smartphone app WeChat 微信[Wei1 xin4])
note: The main place people post personal updates: 发朋友圈 ("post on Moments"). Hiding posts from parents or bosses is common.

gloss: (coll.) to scam sb by setting up an "accident" in which one appears to have sustained damage or injury caused by the scam victim, then demanding compensation (variations include putting "expensive" porcelain in a place where it is likely to be knocked over by passers-by, and stepping into the path of a slow-moving car)
note: Also used figuratively for riding on someone else's fame or picking a fight for attention: 碰瓷名人 ("leech off celebrities").
Officers who clear unlicensed street vendors and enforce city rules. Clashes with vendors have given them a rough public image.

gloss: to seek an audience with higher-ups (esp. government officials) to petition for sth
note: Citizens take grievances to higher levels of government through the 信访 ("letters and visits") system, often travelling to provincial capitals or Beijing.

gloss: to demolish a building and relocate the inhabitants
note: Widespread during urban redevelopment. Compensation can make families rich, hence 拆二代, but forced evictions are a common source of disputes.

gloss: householder who refuses to vacate his home despite pressure from property developers
note: Literally "nail household", one that can't be pulled out. Also used of any holdout who refuses to budge.
Blunt and disapproving, aimed at the woman blamed for breaking up a marriage. 打小三 means confronting her, often in public.
A kept mistress supported with money or a flat, an arrangement long associated with wealthy businessmen and officials.

gloss: (coll.) naive or easily exploited people (esp. small investors or consumers), likened to chives that can be repeatedly harvested for profit
note: Investors' slang: 割韭菜 ("harvest the chives") is fleecing small investors again and again, and losers call themselves 韭菜.

gloss: (slang) (neologism derived from 背黑鍋|背黑锅[bei1 hei1 guo1]) to carry the can; to be a scapegoat
note: Office and online slang for taking the blame for someone else's mistake; 背锅侠 is the person who always ends up blamed.

gloss: (neologism, attested by 2017) to shift the blame; to pass the buck
note: Common in office talk and political commentary. The opposite of 背锅, and the two often appear together.
Now often a trick or manipulative script: 别跟我玩套路 ("don't play games with me"), 套路太深 ("too many tricks").
Mostly disapproving in modern use: 有心机 or 心机女 describes someone calculating and manipulative.
Common slang for doing something with real care: 这礼物很走心 ("a thoughtful gift"). 不走心 means half-hearted.

gloss: it's none of my business ("I’m just here to buy some soy sauce")
note: A catchphrase for being a mere bystander or having a minor role: 我是来打酱油的 ("I'm just passing through").
Online slang for something so bizarre or tasteless it stuns, like being struck by lightning: 雷人的造型 ("an outrageous outfit").

gloss: (vulgar) (of sth that makes one feel misled or let down etc) to be a big disappointment
note: An online exclamation for a letdown or rip-off: 这电影太坑爹了 ("this film is such a letdown"). Crude-sounding but widely used.

gloss: (coll.) cute; adorable (orthographic borrowing from Japanese 萌え "moe", affection for an anime or manga character)
note: Online it covers anything cute, including adults acting cute (卖萌). 萌萌哒 is a gushing way of saying adorable.

gloss: a guy who stays at home all the time, typically spending a lot of time playing online games (derived from Japanese "otaku")
note: Can be self-mocking or dismissive. It usually means an introverted homebody, not specifically an anime fan.

gloss: fan; enthusiast for sb or sth (loanword from "fans")
note: Also the follower count on social media: 粉丝多 ("lots of followers"). A star's fans often go by a collective nickname.
Organised celebrity fandom that buys in bulk, boosts rankings and attacks critics online. Authorities have cracked down on its excesses.

gloss: (neologism c. 2017) (slang) young lady (amiable form of address for a young woman of about one's own age or a little older)
note: A friendly, slightly cute word for a young woman, common online and with strangers. Often preferred to 小姐, which can suggest a sex worker.

gloss: square dancing, an exercise routine performed to music in public squares, parks and plazas, popular esp. among middle-aged and retired women in China
note: Loud music from groups of dancers is a common neighbourhood complaint, and disputes over noise and space make regular news.
Used in exasperation, often online about children who damage things in public, with the parents blamed as 熊家长.
Also 妈宝男. A sharp criticism in dating talk of a man who defers to his mother in everything, including his marriage.

gloss: (Internet slang) guy who grew up in the countryside and gained a foothold in the city through hard work
note: Often critical in marriage talk, implying he puts his rural family's demands before his urban wife. Contrasted with 孔雀女, a city-raised woman.

gloss: (coll.) "leftover man" – a man who remains single beyond the typical marrying age
note: Less of an insult than 剩女. It often points to rural men unable to find wives because of the gender imbalance.
Couples who choose this often face pressure from parents. The word is used as a self-label and in debates about falling birth rates.
The generation born under the one-child policy, in force from about 1980 to 2015. Media often stereotype them as spoiled 小皇帝 ("little emperors").
The official name for state birth limits, chiefly the one-child policy, run by local family planning offices. Not a private choice about contraception.

gloss: "left-behind children", rural children whose parents have to make a living as migrant workers in distant urban areas, but cannot afford to keep the family with them
note: Usually raised by grandparents in the home village. A recognised social problem, regularly covered in news and government policy.
Mostly heard in 空巢老人, elderly people living alone because their children work elsewhere, a common topic in news on ageing.
Best known from 小康社会 ("moderately prosperous society"), the long-running official development goal, declared achieved in 2021.
Mostly done at Spring Festival, when families go round relatives' homes in turn, bringing gifts.

gloss: to pay a New Year call
note: Done in person, by phone or by message during Spring Festival. Children who 拜年 to elders expect a 红包 in return.

gloss: to stay up all night on lunar New Year's Eve
note: A family custom of staying up past midnight together on New Year's Eve, now often in front of the 春晚 TV gala.

gloss: reunion dinner on Lunar New Year's Eve (Chinese New Year tradition)
note: The most important family meal of the year; people travel across the country to be home for it. Fish is served for 年年有余 ("surplus every year").
Set off at New Year, weddings and shop openings to scare off bad luck and make noise. Many cities now ban them.

gloss: Spring Festival couplet (the first line of which is pasted on the right side of a doorway at New Year, and the second on the left side)
note: Written on red paper with lucky wishes and topped by a horizontal 横批 over the door. Put up in the days before New Year.
Traditionally needed for any proper marriage. Today often a relative or neighbour who sets up a 相亲 (arranged blind date).

gloss: to go and live with one's wife's family, in effect becoming a member of her family
note: Traditionally a loss of face for the man, and the children may take the wife's surname. The colloquial word is 倒插门.

gloss: (of the husband) to marry into and live with the wife's family (inverting traditional Chinese expectations)
note: Colloquial and often mocking; the formal word is 入赘. A man who marries in this way still faces some stigma in many places.
Casual and a little jokey, used by men about their wife's father, not to his face. Formal is 岳父.

gloss: adoptive father (traditional adoption, i.e. without legal ramifications)
note: Often a family friend formally taken as a child's godfather. Online it is also slang for a sugar daddy.

gloss: (dialect) close childhood friend whom one grew up with
note: Originally Beijing speech, now widespread: a friend since early childhood, usually from the same street or compound. Closer than 老同学.
Northern and affectionate, used by parents about their own daughter: 我闺女今年上大学 ("my girl starts university this year").
A lifestyle drawn from traditional medicine: herbal teas, eating by season, early nights. 朋克养生 mocks young people doing it half-heartedly.
Things like ginseng, bird's nest and 阿胶, believed in traditional medicine to build strength. Common gifts for elders and new mothers.
Self-applied and fond: 我是个吃货 means "I love my food", with no shame attached. The insult sense is now rare.
A familiar scandal topic in hospitals and public procurement, such as doctors taking 回扣 from drug companies.
Includes gifts to officials, teachers or bosses to get things done, which many see as a social burden. Also covers ordinary gifts when visiting.
Colloquial and contemptuous, usually about flattering bosses. A habitual flatterer is a 马屁精.

gloss: to have one's life made difficult by sb (usu. by sb in a position of authority) (lit. to be made to wear tight shoes)
note: Office politics: 给他穿小鞋 means a superior getting back at someone with petty obstacles and unfair tasks.
A criticism of officials or clerks who answer with rules and stock phrases instead of actually helping.
Common in complaints about officials and companies: giving vague answers and pushing the matter elsewhere.

gloss: (fig.) actions that are technically legal but perhaps not respectable
note: Online, 擦边 often means racy content that stays just inside the rules, such as 擦边视频 on video apps.
A standard complaint about offices that send people back and forth between departments, each saying it is not their job.

gloss: to be made a scapegoat; to be unjustly blamed
note: Online often shortened to 背锅; 甩锅 means pushing blame onto someone else.
Often said of inspections, meetings and campaigns held only for show.

gloss: lit. to cut all at one stroke (idiom); to impose uniformity
note: Almost always a criticism of rules applied rigidly to everyone regardless of local conditions, such as blanket bans.

gloss: excessive concern with form over substance
note: A stock criticism in official Party language, often paired with 官僚主义. Also used of pointless paperwork and meetings at work.
As a description it is a criticism: 太官僚了 means high-handed and unhelpful, not just procedural.
Said of people who act superior and keep others at a distance. 没架子 ("no airs") is praise for an approachable boss or official.

gloss: to do a secret or dishonest deal
note: Using connections or position to get jobs, school places or permits around the rules. 走后门 is the side receiving the favour.

gloss: unspoken rules (usually ones that codify improper behaviors such as leveraging guanxi to get favorable treatment, or coercing employees for sexual favors)
note: Also a verb: 被潜规则 means being pressured into sex in exchange for a role or promotion, especially in show business.
Jokingly, a spouse's secret savings: 老公的小金库 ("hubby's secret stash").
In official language, off-the-books funds kept by a work unit, a regular target of audits and discipline campaigns.
Strongly tied to the campaign begun in 2012, with slogans like 打老虎、拍苍蝇 ("hit tigers and swat flies"), meaning senior and junior officials alike.

gloss: shuanggui, an extralegal system within the CCP for detaining and interrogating cadres who fall from grace
note: Short for requiring a cadre to answer at a set time and place (规定时间、规定地点). Replaced in 2018 by 留置 under the new supervision system.

gloss: to demote a party cadre to work on the shop floor or in the countryside
note: Best known from the Mao era, when cadres and intellectuals were sent to the countryside or factories for labour and reform.

gloss: to redress (an injustice); to rehabilitate (sb whose reputation was unjustly sullied)
note: Used above all for the late 1970s and 1980s, when many people labelled rightists or counterrevolutionaries were officially cleared.
In PRC history, the label given to people targeted in the 1957 Anti-Rightist Campaign. It barred them from normal careers for about two decades.

gloss: model theater (operas and ballets produced during the Cultural Revolution)
note: For years almost the only stage works allowed, beginning with eight approved pieces such as 红灯记. Older people still know the arias.

gloss: coupons for food or grain used in a PRC economic program c. 1955-1993
note: Needed alongside cash to buy grain under rationing. Now a symbol of the planned-economy years and a collector's item.

gloss: household with savings or annual income of 10,000 yuan or more (considered a large amount in the 1970s, when the term became established)
note: A byword for early reform-era wealth. Now used nostalgically or jokingly, given how little 10,000 yuan buys today.
Small family businesses such as stalls, shops and repair stands, which grew in the early reform years and were once looked down on next to state jobs.
Associated with the 1980s, when traders bought scarce goods at low state prices and resold them on the market. Mildly disparaging.

gloss: migrant worker living and working in Beijing or Taipei without a residence permit
note: Mainly about Beijing: young people without a Beijing 户口 who rent cheap rooms to chase work there. Often used of themselves.

gloss: to live (in a tiny, cramped space)
note: Self-mocking word for cramped city housing, made popular by a 2009 TV series of that name about housing prices.
Old villages surrounded by expanding cities, packed with cheap rentals for migrant workers. Many have been demolished for redevelopment.

gloss: a property providing rural accommodation (farm stay, boutique hotel etc)
note: A weekend outing for city people: farm meals, fishing and mahjong at a rural guesthouse near town.

gloss: to go to a local market or country fair (on market day)
note: Rural markets are held on fixed days, often set by the lunar calendar; 赶 conveys hurrying to get there.
Mostly held at Spring Festival, with snacks, folk shows and stalls; in Beijing at parks such as 地坛.

gloss: (used to describe sb or sth that makes a very strong impression, whether favorable or unfavorable) terrible; intense; severe; devastating; amazing; awesome; outstanding
note: Mostly praise in everyday talk: 你真厉害！ ("you're amazing"). Of pain or illness it means severe: 疼得厉害 ("it hurts badly").

gloss: (fig.) to make an extra effort; to cheer sb on
note: The all-purpose cheer, shouted at races and typed before exams or interviews: 加油！ ("come on!", "you can do it").
Often looser than it sounds: a courier's 马上到 ("almost there") can mean several more minutes.
The everyday word husbands use for their wife, casual and affectionate. 妻子 is the written form, and 爱人 sounds older.
Polite and a little old-fashioned on the mainland, more common in Hong Kong and Taiwan: 王太太 ("Mrs Wang"). 阔太太 is a rich man's wife.
Livestreamed selling is big business: 直播带货 means a host selling products live, and the host is a 主播.
Often means a romantic relationship: 感情问题 ("relationship problems"), 他们感情很好 ("they're very close").
An everyday word, not a clinical one: 嗓子发炎 is a sore throat and 伤口发炎 is an infected cut.
A standard report workers and students are expected to write: 年终总结 is the year-end review of one's own work, often required by employers.
Usually with 了: 他已经不在了 ("he's no longer with us"). A gentle way to mention a death, common in speech.
请你吃饭 means the speaker is paying. Older people still greet with 吃饭了吗？ as a hello rather than a question.
The highest level of schooling completed (本科, 硕士), which employers screen on closely. Separate from 学位, the degree actually awarded.
Also the usual word for strays: 流浪猫 and 流浪狗 are stray cats and dogs. 流浪汉 is a homeless man.
Suggests greedy carving up by stronger parties, as when foreign powers sought to 瓜分中国 in the late Qing. Apps also use it for prize pools: 瓜分百万红包.

gloss: to compensate for resting on a workday by working on a holiday
note: Part of the official holiday system, where weekends are turned into workdays to make longer breaks. The practice draws frequent complaints.
Also means time: 没功夫 ("no time"), 一会儿功夫 ("a moment"). 下功夫 means putting real effort into something.
An approving word in official histories: 农民起义 ("peasant uprising"). Rebellions seen as illegitimate are called 叛乱 instead.

Often a required registration with the authorities: websites in mainland China must display an ICP 备案 number.
Covers official review of books, films, games and online posts, before or after release. 过审 means passing it.
The top degree of the imperial examinations, decided by the palace exam in the capital, and the usual route to high office.
In Mao-era politics a label of attack, as in 资产阶级思想 ("bourgeois thinking"). 小资, short for 小资产阶级, now means someone with refined middle-class tastes.

In revolutionary language, a rural landlord or strongman; the slogan 打土豪，分田地 called for seizing their land.
Often based on one's birth date and hour (八字). Some families still consult a fortune-teller about marriage matches or wedding dates.
Online slang for something so bizarre or tasteless it stuns, like being struck by lightning: 雷人的造型 ("an outrageous outfit").
Common slang for doing something with real care: 这礼物很走心 ("a thoughtful gift"). 不走心 means half-hearted.
Blunt and disapproving, aimed at the woman blamed for breaking up a marriage. 打小三 means confronting her, often in public.
A kept mistress supported with money or a flat, an arrangement long associated with wealthy businessmen and officials.

gloss: a home where the kids have grown up and moved out
note: Mostly heard in 空巢老人, elderly people living alone because their children work elsewhere, a common topic in news on ageing.
Best known from 小康社会 ("moderately prosperous society"), the long-running official development goal, declared achieved in 2021.

gloss: to wish sb a Happy New Year
note: Done in person, by phone or by message during Spring Festival. Children who 拜年 to elders expect a 红包 in return.

gloss: to see in the New Year
note: A family custom of staying up past midnight together on New Year's Eve, now often in front of the 春晚 TV gala.
Set off at New Year, weddings and shop openings to scare off bad luck and make noise. Many cities now ban them.
Self-applied and fond: 我是个吃货 means "I love my food", with no shame attached. The insult sense is now rare.
A familiar scandal topic in hospitals and public procurement, such as doctors taking 回扣 from drug companies.
Colloquial and contemptuous, usually about flattering bosses. A habitual flatterer is a 马屁精.

Small family businesses such as stalls, shops and repair stands, which grew in the early reform years and were once looked down on next to state jobs.
Associated with the 1980s, when traders bought scarce goods at low state prices and resold them on the market. Mildly disparaging.

gloss: to migrate to Beijing or Taipei in search of better job opportunities
note: Mainly about Beijing: young people without a Beijing 户口 who rent cheap rooms to chase work there. Often used of themselves.
Self-mocking word for cramped city housing, made popular by a 2009 TV series of that name about housing prices.
